subject: Aviation Meteorology
syllabus_version: Appendix 2.0 B to SA-CATS 61 (ATPL syllabus), section 1.2.1
learning_objective: Atmospheric pressure - explain the relationship between altitude and atmospheric pressure.
question_text: As altitude increases through the lower atmosphere, atmospheric pressure

choices.label: A
choices.text: increases at a constant rate

choices.label: B
choices.text: decreases, most rapidly in the lowest layers

choices.label: C
choices.text: remains constant up to the tropopause

choices.label: D
choices.text: decreases at a constant rate throughout the atmosphere

explanation: Atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude, and the rate of decrease is greatest near the surface (where air density is highest) and becomes progressively smaller with increasing height, since pressure at any level reflects the weight of the air column above it.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Pressure decreases, not increases, with altitude.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Pressure continues to fall through the troposphere and does not remain constant.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: The rate of pressure decrease is not constant; it is non-linear, decreasing more slowly at higher altitudes.

subject: Aviation Meteorology
syllabus_version: Appendix 2.0 B to SA-CATS 61 (ATPL syllabus), section 1.5.3
learning_objective: Density altitude - state the combined effect of high elevation, high temperature, and high humidity on density altitude.
question_text: An aerodrome at high elevation, on a hot day with high humidity, will have a density altitude that is

choices.label: A
choices.text: lower than the field elevation

choices.label: B
choices.text: equal to the field elevation

choices.label: C
choices.text: significantly higher than the field elevation

choices.label: D
choices.text: unaffected by humidity, only by temperature

explanation: High elevation, high temperature, and high humidity all reduce air density, and their effects compound, producing a density altitude significantly higher than the actual field elevation — degrading aircraft performance.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: These conditions raise, not lower, density altitude relative to field elevation.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Density altitude equals field elevation only under standard atmospheric conditions (ISA temperature and pressure), not the hot, humid, high-elevation scenario described.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Humidity does have a (smaller but real) effect on density altitude in addition to temperature and pressure altitude.

subject: Aviation Meteorology
syllabus_version: Appendix 2.0 B to SA-CATS 61 (ATPL syllabus), section 1.6
learning_objective: Adiabatic process, lapse rate and stability - distinguish the dry and saturated adiabatic lapse rates.
question_text: Compared to the dry adiabatic lapse rate (DALR), the saturated adiabatic lapse rate (SALR) is

choices.label: A
choices.text: always steeper (greater cooling rate with height)

choices.label: B
choices.text: always less steep (smaller cooling rate with height), due to the release of latent heat of condensation

choices.label: C
choices.text: identical to the DALR under all conditions

choices.label: D
choices.text: steeper only above the freezing level

explanation: As saturated air rises and cools, condensation releases latent heat into the parcel, partially offsetting the cooling from expansion; this makes the SALR less steep (a smaller temperature decrease per unit height) than the DALR.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The SALR is less steep, not steeper, than the DALR because of latent heat release.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The two lapse rates differ specifically because of the latent heat effect present only when condensation is occurring (saturated air).
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: The SALR/DALR distinction is about saturation, not specifically about the freezing level; the SALR applies whenever the rising air is saturated, regardless of whether it is above or below freezing (with some further variation for the ice-crystal process).

subject: Aviation Meteorology
syllabus_version: Appendix 2.0 B to SA-CATS 61 (ATPL syllabus), section 1.11.3
learning_objective: Thunderstorms - stages of development - identify the stage characterized by the onset of precipitation and coexisting updrafts/downdrafts.
question_text: Which stage of thunderstorm development is characterized by the onset of precipitation reaching the surface, with both updrafts and downdrafts present within the cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cumulus stage

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mature stage

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dissipating stage

choices.label: D
choices.text: Towering cumulus stage

explanation: The mature stage begins when precipitation starts reaching the ground, marking the point at which the cell contains both the original updraft and a newly developed downdraft, producing the storm's most intense weather (heavy rain, lightning, turbulence, possible hail).

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The cumulus stage is dominated by updrafts only, with no precipitation reaching the surface yet.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The dissipating stage is dominated by downdrafts, with the updraft having weakened or ceased.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: 'Towering cumulus stage' is not a standard named stage in the three-stage thunderstorm life-cycle model (cumulus, mature, dissipating).

subject: Aviation Meteorology
syllabus_version: Appendix 2.0 B to SA-CATS 61 (ATPL syllabus), section 1.12
learning_objective: Windshear and turbulence - identify a hazardous low-level windshear scenario on approach.
question_text: An aircraft on final approach in a strong headwind encounters a sudden, significant tailwind component close to the ground. The immediate aerodynamic hazard is a sudden

choices.label: A
choices.text: increase in indicated airspeed and increase in lift, requiring a nose-down correction

choices.label: B
choices.text: decrease in indicated airspeed and loss of lift, risking a sink below the desired flight path

choices.label: C
choices.text: increase in groundspeed only, with no effect on indicated airspeed or lift

choices.label: D
choices.text: decrease in groundspeed and increase in lift

explanation: A headwind-to-tailwind windshear reduces the aircraft's relative airspeed abruptly, causing a sudden loss of lift; close to the ground, this can result in a dangerous sink below the intended approach path with little altitude to recover.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Airspeed and lift decrease, not increase, in this scenario.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Groundspeed does increase, but indicated airspeed and lift are also significantly affected, which is the actual hazard.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Lift decreases, not increases, as airspeed falls.

subject: Aviation Meteorology
syllabus_version: Appendix 2.0 B to SA-CATS 61 (ATPL syllabus), section 1.13.1
learning_objective: Airframe icing - identify the icing type that forms the most rapidly and is aerodynamically most dangerous.
question_text: Which type of airframe ice forms rapidly from large, supercooled water droplets and is considered the most hazardous to an aircraft's aerodynamic performance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rime ice

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clear (glaze) ice

choices.label: C
choices.text: Frost

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hoar ice

explanation: Clear (glaze) ice forms from large supercooled water droplets that spread before freezing, producing a dense, hard, and often irregularly shaped accumulation that seriously disrupts airflow and adds significant weight — generally considered the most hazardous icing type.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Rime ice forms from smaller supercooled droplets that freeze quickly on contact, producing a rough but generally lighter, more brittle, and less aerodynamically disruptive accumulation than clear ice.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Frost forms from direct deposition of water vapour on a surface below freezing (not from droplet impact) and, while hazardous, is a distinct phenomenon from in-flight airframe icing being described here.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: 'Hoar ice' is essentially a synonym for frost, not the droplet-impact icing type described in the question.

subject: Aviation Meteorology
syllabus_version: Appendix 2.0 B to SA-CATS 61 (ATPL syllabus), section 1.15.1
learning_objective: Cold fronts - describe the typical weather associated with a fast-moving cold front.
question_text: A fast-moving cold front is typically associated with

choices.label: A
choices.text: a narrow band of intense weather, possible thunderstorms, and a rapid clearing after passage

choices.label: B
choices.text: a wide band of persistent light rain and slowly lowering cloud extending well ahead of the surface front

choices.label: C
choices.text: no significant weather change at the surface

choices.label: D
choices.text: fog and drizzle extending for several hundred kilometres ahead of the front

explanation: A fast-moving cold front forces warm air upward abruptly along a narrow, steep frontal surface, often producing a narrow band of intense weather (possible thunderstorms, heavy showers, gusty winds), followed by relatively rapid clearing once the front passes.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: A wide band of persistent light rain extending well ahead of the surface position is more characteristic of a warm front, whose shallower slope produces extensive cloud and precipitation ahead of the surface front.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: A significant weather and temperature change at the surface is the defining characteristic of a cold-front passage.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Extensive fog/drizzle hundreds of kilometres ahead of the front is not the fast-moving-cold-front pattern; it more resembles warm-front or occlusion characteristics.

subject: Aviation Meteorology
syllabus_version: Appendix 2.0 B to SA-CATS 61 (ATPL syllabus), section 1.9.3
learning_objective: Cloud classification - distinguish cumuliform from stratiform cloud in terms of the vertical motion that forms them.
question_text: The distinction between cumuliform and stratiform cloud primarily reflects the

choices.label: A
choices.text: altitude at which the cloud forms

choices.label: B
choices.text: type of vertical air motion involved (convective versus widespread gentle lifting)

choices.label: C
choices.text: colour of the cloud base

choices.label: D
choices.text: season in which the cloud is observed

explanation: Cumuliform cloud forms from localized convective (rising) air currents, producing heaped, vertically developed cloud, while stratiform cloud forms from widespread, gentle lifting of a stable air mass, producing flat, layered cloud.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Both cumuliform and stratiform cloud types occur across a range of altitudes (e.g. cumulus vs. stratus at low levels, altocumulus vs. altostratus at mid levels); altitude alone does not define the cumuliform/stratiform distinction.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Cloud base colour is not the classification criterion for cumuliform versus stratiform cloud.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Season is not the defining factor in this classification; the type of vertical motion is.

subject: Aviation Meteorology
syllabus_version: Appendix 2.0 B to SA-CATS 61 (ATPL syllabus), section 1.14.2
learning_objective: Fog - state the conditions favourable to radiation fog formation.
question_text: Radiation fog is most likely to form under which combination of conditions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Clear skies, light winds, and high relative humidity overnight

choices.label: B
choices.text: Overcast skies, strong winds, and low relative humidity overnight

choices.label: C
choices.text: Daytime heating with strong convective activity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rapid frontal passage with heavy precipitation

explanation: Radiation fog forms when the ground cools rapidly through radiative heat loss on a clear night (no cloud to trap heat), with light winds allowing cooling to concentrate near the surface without excessive mixing, and sufficiently high humidity for the air to reach saturation.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Overcast skies trap outgoing radiation and strong winds mix the air, both of which inhibit the surface cooling needed for radiation fog.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Daytime convective heating works against the cooling process that forms radiation fog, which is a nocturnal phenomenon.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Frontal passage and precipitation are associated with other fog/weather types, not the classic radiational-cooling mechanism.

subject: Aviation Meteorology
syllabus_version: Appendix 2.0 B to SA-CATS 61 (ATPL syllabus), section 1.7.3
learning_objective: Formation of wind - state the fundamental cause of wind.

choices.label: A
choices.text: the Earth's rotation alone

choices.label: B
choices.text: horizontal differences in atmospheric pressure, driving air from high to low pressure

choices.label: C
choices.text: differences in humidity between adjacent air masses

choices.label: D
choices.text: the gravitational pull of the moon on the atmosphere

explanation: Wind is fundamentally driven by horizontal pressure gradients: air is pushed from areas of higher pressure toward areas of lower pressure, with the Coriolis force and friction subsequently modifying the resulting flow's direction and speed.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The Earth's rotation (via the Coriolis force) modifies wind direction but is not itself the fundamental driving force; that is the pressure gradient.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Humidity differences influence weather development but are not the fundamental cause of wind.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Lunar gravity drives ocean tides, not atmospheric wind circulation, which is pressure-driven.
